opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think cost has been the missing dimension in agent evaluation, and leaving it out has distorted how we understand progress.

On most agent benchmarks, the leaderboard reports a single number, usually accuracy. But with agents you can almost always buy more accuracy by spending more compute. You can call the model multiple times, have it retry when tests fail, sample many candidate solutions and vote, or let it run longer. So a single accuracy number without cost doesn't tell you much. It's like comparing cars by top speed without asking what fuel they use or what they cost.

When we looked at this carefully, we found that some fairly simple baselines, like retrying a model a few times or slowly raising the temperature, could match or beat elaborate, heavily hyped agent architectures on certain coding benchmarks, at a fraction of the cost. That should give us pause. If we can't show that the complex system is actually better at a given cost, it's hard to claim it represents real progress rather than just spending more.

So my main recommendation is to treat evaluation as a two-dimensional problem. Plot accuracy against cost and look at the Pareto frontier: which systems give you the best accuracy for a given budget, or the lowest cost for a given accuracy. That's a much more honest picture, and it matches how people actually deploy these things.

There's a subtlety about which cost to measure, though. There's the one-time cost of designing or optimizing the agent, and the variable cost of running it on each task. For a researcher, the fixed cost might matter. For a downstream developer running the agent millions of times, the per-query cost dominates. Different audiences need different views, so benchmarks should report enough for people to make their own judgment.

People sometimes say cost doesn't matter because inference prices keep falling. Prices are falling, but that argument cuts both ways. If costs drop, we can afford to make agents run longer and try more things, so the trade-off stays. And in real deployments, a system that's slightly more accurate but ten times more expensive is often just not viable.

More broadly, this is part of a bigger concern I have: agent benchmarks are often built for comparing models, not for telling a developer whether an agent will be useful and cost-effective in their application. Accounting for cost is one of the simplest and most important steps toward closing that gap.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sampling candidate solutions and voting, but does not say a correctness oracle selects a correct solution from the samples.

r002.rationale: It says accuracy without cost is not informative and questions whether a complex system shows real progress unless it performs better at a given cost.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends plotting accuracy against cost and examining the Pareto frontier.

r004.rationale: It says retries can match or beat elaborate systems at lower cost, but does not clearly state that repeated attempts are often the simplest way to maximize performance within a fixed budget.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think cost has been the missing dimension in agent evaluation, and the reason comes down to how agents differ from the models we've been benchmarking for years.

With a language model, you send a prompt and get a response, and the cost per query is roughly fixed. With an agent, that's not true at all. An agent can call the model five times or five hundred times. It can spawn subagents, retry on failure, run tool calls in a loop. So if I only report accuracy, I'm hiding a variable that can span two or three orders of magnitude. Two agents can both score, say, seventy percent on a benchmark, and one of them costs a few cents per task while the other costs tens of dollars. From a leaderboard's perspective those look identical. From a practitioner's perspective they're completely different products.

What we found when we looked at this, with Sayash Kapoor and others in my group, is that a lot of the apparent progress on agent benchmarks was coming from things like running the model many times and taking a majority vote, or very elaborate scaffolding that drove up inference cost enormously. And when you actually plot accuracy against cost, a surprising amount of that sophistication gets dominated by very simple baselines. Just retrying a plain model a handful of times, or using a slightly better model with a minimal scaffold, often lands on the Pareto frontier. The complex agent architectures frequently did not.

So my view is that evaluation should be fundamentally two-dimensional. You report accuracy and you report cost, and you look at the Pareto frontier rather than a single number. Anything that isn't on that frontier is, in a meaningful sense, not a contribution to the state of the art, even if its raw accuracy is high.

There's a second-order issue too, which is that the right cost metric depends on who you are. If you're a model developer, you care about something like token counts or compute, because dollar prices are set by vendors and change over time. If you're a downstream developer deploying an agent, you care about dollars, because that's what hits your budget. Benchmarks have mostly been designed by and for researchers, and they've imported the researcher's perspective, where cost is an afterthought. We've argued those are really two different audiences with two different evaluation needs, and conflating them is part of why the field has been confused.

And then there's a reproducibility point. If cost isn't a first-class reported quantity, you get agents that are tuned to the benchmark in ways that no one would ever deploy, because they'd be unaffordable. The benchmark score stops being predictive of real-world usefulness. Making cost explicit is a kind of forcing function that keeps evaluation honest about what's actually usable.

So the short version is: don't treat cost as a footnote. Treat accuracy and cost as jointly the thing you're measuring, and be clear about whose cost you mean.

r001.rationale: The response mentions majority voting and retries, but does not specify code generation or a correctness oracle selecting a correct solution.

r002.rationale: It says cost can make equally accurate agents very different products and that an agent off the accuracy–cost frontier is not meaningfully a state-of-the-art contribution.

r003.rationale: It explicitly proposes reporting accuracy and cost together and evaluating agents by the Pareto frontier.

r004.rationale: It says a handful of retries can reach the Pareto frontier, but does not state that repeated attempts maximize performance within a fixed cost budget.

astra-6.text:
I think cost has to be a first-class part of the evaluation. If you tell me an agent gets a higher success rate on a benchmark, but it spends ten times as much to do that, I want to know how much of the improvement comes from a better approach and how much comes from simply taking more attempts.

Even a very simple strategy—try again when you fail—can improve performance if you give it enough compute and have a reliable way to check whether it succeeded. So accuracy alone can give us a misleading picture of progress.

What I’d like to see is the tradeoff between cost and success rate. Compare agents at the same budget, or ask how cheaply each agent can reach a given level of performance. That makes the evaluation much more useful for someone deciding whether to deploy one. The question becomes: can this agent do the task reliably at a cost that makes sense?

r001.rationale: The response says retrying can improve performance when success can be checked, but it does not specify a code-generating agent or selecting a correct solution from generated samples.

r002.rationale: It says success-rate claims can mislead when an agent spends much more, and argues that cost must be part of performance evaluation.

r003.rationale: It proposes comparing cost against success rate, including comparing agents at equal budgets or comparing the cost to reach a given performance level.

r004.rationale: It calls retrying a simple strategy, but does not say repeated attempts are the simplest way to maximize performance within a fixed cost budget.

sol-6.1.text:
I think cost has to be part of the definition of performance, rather than something we look at afterward. An agent can get a higher success rate simply by making more attempts, calling the model more times, or using a more expensive model. That might be useful, but it doesn’t necessarily mean we’ve built a better agent.

So instead of asking only, “What fraction of tasks did it solve?” we should ask, “What fraction did it solve at a given cost?” Ideally, you’d show a curve: as you give the agent more budget, how much does its success rate improve? Then you can compare systems at the same budget, or compare what it costs them to reach the same level of reliability.

That also changes what we optimize for. A relatively simple approach might be preferable if it achieves nearly the same accuracy at a fraction of the cost. And for someone actually deploying these systems, that tradeoff is often much more informative than a single number on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: It says more attempts can raise success, but does not mention code generation or a correctness oracle selecting a correct solution from samples.

r002.rationale: It argues that success alone does not establish a better agent and says performance comparisons should account for inference cost.

r003.rationale: It proposes plotting success rate against budget and comparing systems at equal budgets or equal reliability, expressing the accuracy–cost tradeoff.

r004.rationale: It mentions more attempts as one way to improve success, but does not say repeated attempts are often the simplest way to maximize performance within a fixed budget.
